I build software by telling AI agents what to build. I describe it in plain English, I playtest everything myself, and I check the work before I call it done. These pages are my projects and how they got made. If you are starting out with this stuff, take what is useful. I am also training to be an electrician. That runs alongside all of this.

Salvage Bots

POST-APOCALYPSE AUTOFIRE · PROTOTYPE, STATED PLAINLY

A salvage robot holds a scrapyard town against waves of junk-built bots. Autofire combat, chained maps, minibosses guarding every door, and a 1-of-3 mod choice on every kill. Not a commercial release. It is a prototype, and I say that up front. I have spent more time on this one than anything else here. Most of its bugs were found by me playing it, not by tests.

SYSTEMSIN USE

Beehive

Beehive is my attempt at an assistant that runs on my own machine instead of somebody else's servers. A chat I can keep going indefinitely, that remembers what matters, on a small local model with a small window. And a developer that works from my description. I say what I want built. The system plans it and builds it. I check the result. Every job leaves a full record of what the agent did, and I decide what counts.

Start here if you want agents on real code and do not want to take their word for anything.

03 — THE METHOD

By feel — with the receipts

I did not get this from a book.
It came out of doing it over and over and keeping the parts that caught problems.

  1. 01

    Describe it in plain English

    I describe what I want in normal words. That gets me a build I can play in minutes. I do not write big spec documents for this.

  2. 02

    Pool ideas, build on “go”

    New ideas go in a pool. Ideas go on a list. Nothing gets built until I say go. That keeps me from starting five things and finishing none of them.

  3. 03

    Play it and judge it by hand

    I play every build myself. Bad spawn placement, falling through the world, a wave of enemies stuck outside a wall. Tests did not catch those. Playing did.

  4. 04

    Settle arguments by playing

    If I cannot settle it by arguing, I build it both ways and play both. Playing settles it faster than thinking does.

  5. 05

    Write the numbers down

    When something feels right, I write the number down. The game has tuning dials I can export. 54 of them, set by playing, are now the defaults the game ships with.

  6. 06

    Verify, then hand it back

    A fix is not done when the builder says so. It comes back with checks run, and then I play it again. If the problem is still there, it goes back.
